strengths: UNOT addresses a useful problem: amortizing entropic OT computation across distributions and image resolutions for a fixed cost. Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated training measures, and short Sinkhorn refinement targets is a meaningful contribution even though the individual components are established.

The reported initialization gains are substantial across several datasets and cross-dataset pairs. For example, Table 1 reduces the mean iterations needed for 1% transport-cost error from 80 to 3 on CIFAR and from 78 to 7 on LFW. Table 2 reports practical speedups reaching 3.46x, while transparently showing a slowdown on MNIST.

The appendix extends evaluation through resolution and regularization sweeps and marginal-constraint measurements. Barycenter, interpolation, and particle-flow examples provide encouraging evidence that the learned potentials have uses beyond scalar cost prediction.

The contraction-based residual bound in Proposition 5 provides a reasonable motivation for bootstrapped targets. Architecture descriptions, training hyperparameters, pseudocode, and a link to code and model weights also aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claimed generator universality is not established for the implemented model. Appendix C explicitly uses a 200-dimensional latent input for 8192 output coordinates and does not enforce the Lipschitz constraint required by Theorem 3. The theorem therefore cannot justify the assertion that training coverage is unrestricted. Moreover, Corollary 4 is false as stated: G1(z)=ReLU(z/2+1) and G2(z)=ReLU(z/2) satisfy its architectural assumptions, but G1(G2(z)) is always at least 1 and cannot cover the positive half-line. Although this corollary is not needed by the implementation, it requires correction.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the contribution relative to the closest prior work. Amos et al. is excluded because of dataset dependence, but a fixed-resolution comparison using the same synthetic training pairs would be informative. Controlled ablations of adversarial versus non-adversarial generation and bootstrapping versus the existing dual-objective loss are also missing. The brief MLP discussion does not replace these comparisons. Consequently, it remains unclear which proposed components produce the gains.

Several mathematical conventions need reconciliation. Equation (1) subtracts KL divergence, whereas standard entropic OT adds it; this appears to be a repairable sign error. More consequentially, Algorithm 1 reports only the transport term while calling it OT_epsilon, whereas Appendix A.7 includes entropy. Proposition 1 also identifies scaling potentials with the product-measure dual potentials without the required marginal-dependent adjustments. These inconsistencies obscure the evaluated quantity and the connection between the convergence theorem and the learned outputs.

The barycenter algorithm is incorrect as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to the current probability vector minus its gradient. Even with a zero gradient, this changes a nonuniform distribution, so a nonuniform optimum need not be a fixed point. The actual projection, logit parametrization, or mirror-descent update must be specified before the barycenter results can be reproduced reliably.

The claims about accurately capturing Wasserstein geometry and outperforming GeONet rely primarily on selected visual examples. Figure 14 usefully measures marginal feasibility, but this does not establish transport-plan accuracy. Aggregate barycenter objective gaps, interpolation errors, and a quantitative GeONet comparison would substantially strengthen these conclusions.

Proposition 5 establishes a residual-to-error bound, not convergence of the detached-target adversarial training algorithm. Driving the residual to zero would control prediction error, but decreasing it does not necessarily decrease the actual error, and maximizing it need not identify the largest true errors. The kernel-dependent constant can also become extremely loose at small regularization. The optimization claims should be narrowed accordingly.

The runtime evidence supports acceleration over the reported default implementation, but does not establish state-of-the-art runtime performance. Gaussian initialization timings are omitted, and speedups from prior publications are compared without matched hardware and implementations. Together with the missing learned baseline and the theoretical and algorithmic issues above, this makes weak rejection more appropriate despite the promising empirical results.
